newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Blast kills 11 mourners in Moscow cemetery.
newsitem.headline: Blast kills 11 mourners in Moscow cemetery.

text.p: At least 11 people were killed when a powerful bomb explosion ripped through a crowd of mourners at a commemorative service in a Moscow cemetery on Sunday. One victim was hurled 30 metres (yards) through the air.
Security officials said the dead included the widow of Mikhail Likhodei, a controversial figure whose murder in a bomb blast on November 10, 1994, was being recalled.

Colonel Stanislav Zhorin of the Federal Security Service said Likhodei's successor as head of the Afghan War Invalids' Foundation (eds: correct) was also killed by a blast which left a crater more than a metre deep and nearly four metres wide.

"It was probably linked to a settling of old scores," Zhorin todl reporters, referring to a dispute between rival Afghan war veteran organisations which have big tax exemptions to ease their commercial activities.

He said about 130 people had gathered on Sunday morning at the Kotlyakovskoye cemetery in southern Moscow to pay their respects to Likhodei when an explosive device wired to a control some 40 metres (yards) away went off.
The force of the explosion was the equivalent of about two to three kg of TNT, he said.
Zhorin said 11 people had been taken to hospital. Russian news agency reports had initially put the number of wounded at up to 70.
I saw a mutilated body lying on a grave some 30 metres from the centre of the blast.
Scores of officials sealed off the blast site and used special equipment to scan the adjourning alleys in a search for any evidence and other explosive devices.
When Likhodei was killed by a remote control bomb in 1994, his wife Yelena and two bodyguards were injured, Itar-Tass news agency said. Police have not yet solved the case.
The head of another Afghan war veterans' group which was involved in a dispute with Likhodei's group was recently wounded in an apparent assassination attempt, Interfax news agency said.

The incident was the latest in a series of explosions and gangland murders which have rocked Moscow during a difficult transition to a free market economy, which has been accompanied by a surge in the crime rate.
U.S. businessman Paul Tatum was shot dead in a hail of automatic gunfire at the entrance to a Moscow underground station on November 3.
Tatum, whose company Americom was locked in a bitter legal battle over ownership of the Radisson-Slavjanskaya hotel in central Moscow, died of wounds in hospital.
The gunman fled in a car after dropping a submachinegun at the Kievskaya metro station next to the Radisson-Slavjanskaya, where U.S. President Bill Clinton has stayed.
Contract killings of bankers, businessmen and even members of national and local parliaments are nearly an everyday affair in Russia. Most of them remain unresolved.
